design_note: Test a payment-service invariant independently of an attractive runtime outcome. A deliberately torn test fixture has a legal balance but lacks the key-to-receipt record, exposing why balance correctness alone cannot establish recoverable effect identity.

source.title: Atomic Commit In SQLite
source.concept: A transaction commits its changes together or none at all. Crash testing verifies the recovered database against this all-or-nothing condition.
source.scope: Original deliberately broken payment fixture illustrates an application invariant. It is not a SQLite failure report, executed test result or claim about distributed atomicity.

lesson.anchor: Stage 8: packaging the harness as reusable interfaces
lesson.title: A valid balance can conceal a torn effect record
lesson.intro: A deliberately broken payment test fixture commits its refunded balance but omits the key receipt. The shipped companion instead commits both atomically. These constructed records describe a contract defect to detect.

data.result: Fail the service contract test; retain uncertainty.

read: The balance passes its local numeric invariant.
The missing key receipt breaks the promised attribution and recovery contract.
A correct fixture commits balance and key result in the same transaction.
lesson.question: Does the passing balance check alone establish that K-17 can be recovered correctly?
lesson.answer: No. It shows only that the stored refunded amount is within the captured balance. The missing receipt cannot establish which operation produced it or return the promised result for K-17. Fail this fixture and repair the atomic service transaction; do not infer successful recovery from the balance alone.
lesson.takeaway: Verify the complete transaction invariant, including the evidence needed for recovery.
lesson.assumption: Constructed broken fixture, not a reported test run. Correct SQLite transaction behavior depends on its supported storage and durability assumptions; databases remain separate.
